after.label: Historical economics
after.description: Historical economists investigate the changing institutions and conditions within which economic claims hold. German programmes, British disciplinary formation, and empirical price research overlap but differ. Their debates concern how to combine explanation and historical evidence: Toynbee values conditional deduction, while Schmoller disputes Menger’s account of abstraction.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Gustav Schmoller; William Ashley; William Cunningham; Arnold Toynbee. Thorold Rogers supplies a related empirical tradition in prices and wages. Contextual readings now distinguish Roscher’s 1843 programme, Schmoller’s 1883 methodological review, Cunningham’s textbook, Ashley’s medieval studies, Toynbee’s lectures, Rogers’s wage research and Menger’s criticism.

after.label: Political economy & economic theory
after.date_label: Classical and later nineteenth-century roots; subsequent historical adaptations
after.description: A contested body of explanation about production, distribution and exchange. Smith’s division of labour, Ricardo’s distribution problem, Mill’s institutional distinctions, Marshall’s treatment of markets and time, and Menger’s account of theory offer different resources. Historians adapt and criticize these arguments rather than inheriting one uniform model.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Adam Smith is an eighteenth-century precursor; Ricardo, Mill, and Marshall represent different nineteenth-century developments. This is not a single unchanging paradigm. Read Smith (1776), Ricardo (1817/1821), Mill (1848), Marshall (1890/1920), and Menger’s methodological intervention (1883) as differing arguments, not a linear succession.

historicalecon.people: Reviewed all five inherited selections; added Roscher as an earlier German precursor and Menger explicitly as a critic. Distinct British and German programmes remain visible; further historical-school figures are a bounded follow-up.
